title: You are my father
hook: You are my father, You are my mother, You my kin and my brother (Majh M5, ang 103)

segments.voice: Yesterday, partners: everyone holds a share in the same grace. Today, a few pages on in Guru Arjan's Majh hymns, partners become family.

Father. Mother. Kin. Brother. Four plain family words, one after another: that's how this hymn of Guru Arjan opens. A child could sing that list after one hearing. An adult sitting in a hospital corridor at three in the morning could say it too, and mean something a child can't yet know. The words stay the same; the person singing them keeps changing.
screen: `FOUR PLAIN FAMILY WORDS.` → `A CHILD COULD SING IT.` → `SO COULD A HOSPITAL CORRIDOR.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Majh, on ang 103. It begins, in effect: You are my father, You are my mother. You are my kin, You are my brother. You are my protector in every place, so what fear, what worry, can touch me? The second stanza: by Your grace I come to know You. You are my shelter, You are my honor. Without You there is no other; all of this is Your play, Your arena. Listen for two words there: ot, shelter, and maan, honor. We met them in the Ardas three weeks ago: the honor of the dishonored, the shelter of the shelterless. Here Guru Arjan says them in the first person: You are my shelter, You are my honor. Why family words? Guru Arjan had a father and mother. He had brothers, and one of them, Prithi Chand, tradition says, kept back his letters home. Families hold the deepest love and sometimes the deepest hurt, and the shabad doesn't pretend otherwise. What it does is name the One as every kind of family at once: the father who provides, the mother who holds, the kin who belong to you, the brother who stands next to you. Whatever a person has or lacks in their own family, the hymn offers the same thing: you are not without family. And from there it reasons straight to fearlessness. If the One is all of these, everywhere, fear has nowhere to stand. That's not a promise that nothing hard will happen. In the hymn, it's a promise about who is there when it does.
screen: `FATHER, MOTHER, KIN, BROTHER.` · `MY PROTECTOR IN EVERY PLACE.` · `OT AND MAAN, AS IN THE ARDAS.` · `SO WHAT FEAR CAN TOUCH ME?` · then, large: `YOU ARE MY FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Let the family words come one at a time, father, mother, kin, brother, and with each, notice what rises: warmth, ache, absence, gratitude, whatever it is. If you pray, you can say the line to the One slowly, in English or Punjabi: You are my father, You are my mother. If you don't, simply rest with the thought that you are not without family, and let one person who has been family to you come to mind.
Pitaa, father: Guru Arjan names the One as pitaa, mother, kin and brother, protector everywhere, and asks, so what fear can touch me?
Your line: you are my family. Ot and maan, shelter and honor, said in the first person. Six hundred fifty-three days, and counting.

howItsDone: Guru Arjan's 'toon meraa pitaa toonhai meraa maataa' is sung in kirtan, taught to children, and turned to in times of trouble.

what a scholar hears: Guru Arjan's second stanza reuses ot and maan, terms that later frame the Ardas's nimaaniaan de maan, niotiaan di ot; the kinship list moves to raakhaa, protector, and an argument for fearlessness.

chat.says: Why would a hymn call God father and mother and brother all at once?
options: So nobody is without family: the One is all of it, so what fear can touch me?
It means your own family no longer matters once you have faith.
It's a list of the Gurus' own relatives, honored in the hymn by name.
